concept.name: Columnar Analytics Engines

relationships.description: Connects Columnar Analytics Engines to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Storage and execution engines that lay out data by column rather than row, cutting OLAP disk I/O by 90%+ and hitting 10x–20x compression via dictionary encoding, RLE, and vectorized SIMD scans.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use columnar engines (ClickHouse, DuckDB, Parquet) for wide-table aggregations and time-series scans, but keep single-row OLTP updates in row stores.

concept.whyItMatters: Row-oriented databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) store every column of a tuple contiguously on 8KB/16KB pages. Running `SELECT SUM(revenue) FROM events WHERE day = '2026-11-01'` on a 120-column table forces a row store to read all 120 columns off disk, wasting 97%+ of I/O bandwidth and CPU cache lines. Columnar engines store each column in contiguous blocks, reading only the 2–3 referenced columns and executing tight SIMD loops over compressed arrays.
whenToUse: OLAP aggregations, funnel analytics, and observability logs scanning millions to billions of rows across a subset of columns.
Data lakehouse storage (Apache Parquet / Iceberg on S3/GCS) queried by DuckDB, Trino, or Spark where storage cost and scan bandwidth dominate.
Real-time user-facing dashboards requiring sub-100ms p95 `GROUP BY` and percentile queries over append-heavy event streams.
whenNotToUse: High-concurrency OLTP workloads doing thousands of single-row `INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE` operations by primary key (e.g., banking ledgers, user profiles).
Point lookups that return all 80+ columns of a single record (`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?`), where row stores require only 1 B-Tree page read.
Low-latency transactional workflows requiring multi-row ACID locks across arbitrary tables.
keyPoints: Projection pushdown skips unreferenced columns entirely; predicate pushdown uses per-block min/max zone maps and Bloom filters to skip entire 64MB row groups or 8,192-row granules.

Homogeneous column data enables extreme compression: Dictionary encoding maps repeated strings to integers, Run-Length Encoding (RLE) collapses sorted runs, and Delta/Frame-of-Reference (FOR) packs timestamps before ZSTD/LZ4.
Vectorized execution (DuckDB, ClickHouse, Velox) processes batches of 1,024–4,096 values per column in L1/L2 CPU cache, avoiding tuple-at-a-time virtual function call overhead.
LSM-tree / immutable part architectures (ClickHouse MergeTree, Parquet files) batch writes into large sequential flushes and merge small parts asynchronously in the background.
Sort key (`ORDER BY`) design determines both query speed via sparse primary indexes and compression ratio via RLE on leading low-cardinality columns.

examples.title: Sub-100ms Ad-Tech Funnel Queries in ClickHouse
examples.scenario: An ad-tech platform ingests 50,000 events/sec (120 columns per event) and needs sub-second cohort breakdowns by `tenant_id`, `campaign_id`, and `event_date`.
examples.outcome: Storing data in ClickHouse `MergeTree` partitioned by `toYYYYMM(event_date)` with `ORDER BY (tenant_id, campaign_id, event_date)` keeps the sparse 8,192-row primary index under 200MB in RAM. Queries touching 4 columns scan 96% less data than PostgreSQL and complete in 65ms p95 with 14:1 ZSTD compression.

examples.title: Zero-ETL Lakehouse Analytics with DuckDB over Parquet
examples.scenario: A data engineering team stores 4TB of daily order logs as ZSTD-compressed Apache Parquet files in S3 and needs fast ad-hoc joins without provisioning a Spark cluster.
examples.outcome: DuckDB reads Parquet footer metadata, applies HTTP range requests to fetch only the 3 needed columns and matching row groups (128MB each), and executes vectorized hash joins in-process on a single 16-core VM in 3.2 seconds.

tradeOffs.pro: Sequential columnar reads and SIMD vectorization deliver 10x–100x faster analytical aggregations.
tradeOffs.con: Updating or deleting a single row requires rewriting immutable column files or maintaining expensive delete bitmaps/tombstones.

tradeOffs.pro: Sorting by low-cardinality columns first (e.g., `country`, `event_type`) maximizes RLE compression and range pruning.
tradeOffs.con: Queries filtering only on trailing high-cardinality columns (e.g., `user_uuid`) cannot use the sparse prefix index and degrade to full scans.

tradeOffs.pro: Batching 10k–100k rows per insert creates large parts with minimal background merge overhead.
tradeOffs.con: Micro-batching adds 1–5 seconds of ingestion latency compared to immediate single-row OLTP commits.

failureModes.name: Too Many Parts (Small-Insert Storm)
failureModes.description: Sending 1,000 single-row INSERTs per second into ClickHouse or Iceberg creates thousands of tiny immutable files, exhausting file descriptors and stalling background merges.
failureModes.mitigation: Buffer writes in Kafka, Vector, or `async_insert=1` and flush in batches of 10,000–100,000 rows every 1–5 seconds.

failureModes.name: High-Cardinality GROUP BY OOM
failureModes.description: Grouping by an unindexed high-cardinality key like `session_id` or `url` across 500M rows blows past per-query memory limits during hash aggregation.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable external disk spill (`max_bytes_before_external_group_by`), pre-aggregate via materialized views, or use approximate sketches (`uniqHLL12`).

failureModes.name: SELECT * Defeating Column Pruning
failureModes.description: Application ORMs or BI tools issuing `SELECT *` on a 150-column Parquet/ClickHouse table force decompression of every column, erasing the columnar advantage.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce explicit column projections in query builders and create narrow projection views for BI dashboards.

failureModes.name: Unmerged Duplicate Rows in ReplacingMergeTree
failureModes.description: Expecting immediate deduplication on `ReplacingMergeTree` or Iceberg equality deletes before background compaction finishes causes double-counted metrics.
failureModes.mitigation: Query with `FINAL` (or `argMax` aggregations) on small windows, or run scheduled compaction before downstream SLA reporting.

commonMistakes: Choosing `UUID` or `timestamp_ms` as the leading column in `ORDER BY`, which destroys RLE compression and forces full-partition scans for tenant queries.
Leaving Parquet row groups at 1MB–5MB instead of 128MB–256MB, causing excessive S3 GET requests and poor dictionary/ZSTD ratios.
Partitioning tables by high-cardinality keys like `user_id` or `hour` instead of `day` or `month`, creating millions of tiny metadata files.
Running OLTP-style `UPDATE ... WHERE id = ?` mutations in a loop against a columnar store instead of append-only event logs or CDC.
Ignoring memory limits on vectorized hash joins when joining two large fact tables without broadcast hints or sort-merge.

sections.content:
## The idea

Columnar analytics engines invert physical storage layout from row-major (storing all fields of row 1, then row 2) to column-major (storing all values of column A together, then all values of column B). Because analytical queries typically aggregate 2 to 5 columns across millions of rows, columnar storage eliminates up to 95%+ of unnecessary disk and network I/O. Storing identical data types contiguously also unlocks lightweight encodings—Dictionary, Run-Length Encoding (RLE), and Delta—followed by ZSTD/LZ4 compression and SIMD vectorized execution directly in CPU cache.

## Concrete walkthrough

Suppose a 100-column `orders` table holds 500 million rows (600 GB uncompressed). We run:
`SELECT country, SUM(amount_cents) FROM orders WHERE created_date >= '2026-11-01' AND status = 'PAID' GROUP BY country;`

1. **Metadata Pruning**: The engine reads the Parquet file footers or ClickHouse `primary.idx` sparse index (1 entry per 8,192 rows). Min/max zone maps on `created_date` immediately skip 92% of row groups/granules from earlier months.
2. **Column Projection**: Only 4 columns (`created_date`, `status`, `country`, `amount_cents`) are fetched via S3 byte-range requests or mmap—ignoring the other 96 columns (JSON payloads, shipping addresses, user agents).
3. **Late Materialization & Vectorized Filter**: The engine decompresses `status` (dictionary-encoded as 1-byte integers), evaluates `status == 'PAID'` using a tight SIMD loop into a 2,048-bit selection vector, and only decompresses `amount_cents` for matching rows.
4. **In-Cache Aggregation**: `country` and `amount_cents` are aggregated in an L2-cache-resident hash table, returning the result in ~80ms instead of 40+ seconds.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Encoding pipelines and sparse primary indexes
sections.content:
## Encoding pipelines and sparse primary indexes

Columnar compression happens in two stages: **type-specific logical encoding** followed by **general-purpose block compression (LZ4 or ZSTD)**:
- **Dictionary Encoding**: Replaces repeated strings (e.g., `country`, `status`, `device_os`) with compact integer IDs, shrinking 16-byte strings to 1-byte or 2-byte codes.
- **Run-Length Encoding (RLE)**: When sorted by `ORDER BY (tenant_id, event_date)`, thousands of identical `tenant_id` values collapse into a single `(value, count)` pair.
- **Delta + Bit-Packing**: Monotonic timestamps (`1730419200`, `1730419201`, ...) are stored as small deltas (`+1`, `+1`) packed into 2–4 bits each.

Unlike OLTP B-Trees that index every single row (consuming tens of GBs of RAM), engines like ClickHouse use a **sparse primary index** recording only 1 key per 8,192-row granule. A 1-billion-row table requires only ~122,000 index entries, fitting effortlessly in L3 cache or a few megabytes of RAM.

## Columnar engine & format comparison

| Engine / Format | Architecture | Best Workload | Compression / Index | Update Model |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **ClickHouse** | Distributed shared-nothing `MergeTree` | Real-time OLAP dashboards, logs, metrics (<100ms) | LZ4/ZSTD + 8,192-row sparse index + skipping indexes | Immutable parts merged asynchronously; `ReplacingMergeTree` |
| **DuckDB** | Embedded in-process vectorized OLAP | Local/S3 Parquet analytics, Python/SQL ETL (GBs–TBs) | Reads Parquet/Arrow directly; 2048-tuple vectors | Append/copy-on-write MVCC for local `.duckdb` files |
| **Apache Parquet** | Open-source immutable file format | Data lakes (S3/GCS) with Iceberg/Delta Lake | 128MB row groups, Dictionary/RLE + ZSTD/Snappy | Append-only; updates via Iceberg delete files or rewrite |
| **PostgreSQL (Row)** | 8KB heap pages + B-Tree indexes | OLTP transactions, point lookups, multi-row locks | TOAST compression (>2KB values); dense B-Trees | In-place MVCC tuple versions + VACUUM |

## Failure modes

- **Unbatched insert fragmentation**: Inserting 1 row per HTTP request creates thousands of tiny parts/files, triggering `Too many parts` errors in ClickHouse or metadata bloat in Iceberg.
- **Poor `ORDER BY` key selection**: Putting a high-cardinality UUID first in the sort key prevents RLE compression and forces full-table scans for tenant-scoped queries.
- **Materialized view write amplification**: Attaching 10+ synchronous `MATERIALIZED VIEW` targets to an ingest table multiplies CPU and I/O on every batch insert.
- **Clock-skewed partitioning**: Partitioning by client-generated timestamps without bounds creates thousands of stray historical/future partitions (e.g., year `1970` or `2099`).

## Query execution and materialization

To keep p95 latency predictable under concurrent dashboard load:
- **Pre-aggregate with Incremental Materialized Views**: Roll up raw 50k RPS clickstreams into 1-minute `SummingMergeTree` or `AggregatingMergeTree` tables using `AggregateFunction(quantiles(0.95), latency_ms)` states.
- **Data Skipping Indexes**: Add `minmax` or `bloom_filter(0.01)` secondary skipping indexes on high-cardinality filter columns like `trace_id` or `order_id` that are not in the primary `ORDER BY` prefix.
- **Zero-Copy Arrow Interchange**: Use Apache Arrow Flight or DuckDB-to-Pandas/Polars zero-copy buffers when feeding analytical slices into ML feature pipelines, avoiding JSON/CSV serialization overhead.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Order `ORDER BY` / sort keys from lowest-cardinality common filter to highest-cardinality (e.g., `(tenant_id, event_type, toDate(ts), user_id)`).
- [ ] Batch all writes to at least 10,000–100,000 rows per flush (or 128MB–256MB Parquet row groups).
- [ ] Partition by coarse time intervals (`toYYYYMM` or `toYYYYMMDD`)—never by `user_id` or `hour`.
- [ ] Replace `SELECT *` in application queries and BI tools with explicit column projections.
- [ ] Pre-aggregate recurring 95th-percentile and count-distinct queries via incremental materialized views or HyperLogLog sketches.
- [ ] Enforce per-query memory limits and disk-spill thresholds so a single runaway `GROUP BY` cannot OOM-kill the node.

interviewProblems.title: Columnar Analytics Engines
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Columnar Analytics Engines. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Storage and execution engines that lay out data by column rather than row, cutting OLAP disk I/O by 90%+ and hitting 10x–20x compression via dictionary encoding, RLE, and vectorized SIMD scans.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Columnar Files applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Vectorized Executor.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Vectorized Executor experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Buffer writes in Kafka, Vector, or `async_insert=1` and flush in batches of 10,000–100,000 rows every 1–5 seconds.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use columnar engines (ClickHouse, DuckDB, Parquet) for wide-table aggregations and time-series scans, but keep single-row OLTP updates in row stores.
Avoid trap: Choosing `UUID` or `timestamp_ms` as the leading column in `ORDER BY`, which destroys RLE compression and forces full-partition scans for tenant queries.
Avoid trap: Leaving Parquet row groups at 1MB–5MB instead of 128MB–256MB, causing excessive S3 GET requests and poor dictionary/ZSTD ratios.
When to reach for it: OLAP aggregations, funnel analytics, and observability logs scanning millions to billions of rows across a subset of columns.
When to reach for it: Data lakehouse storage (Apache Parquet / Iceberg on S3/GCS) queried by DuckDB, Trino, or Spark where storage cost and scan bandwidth dominate.

putItTogether.title: Putting Columnar Analytics Engines Together
putItTogether.summary: Use columnar engines (ClickHouse, DuckDB, Parquet) for wide-table aggregations and time-series scans, but keep single-row OLTP updates in row stores.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Columnar Analytics Engines before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Storing data in ClickHouse `MergeTree` partitioned by `toYYYYMM(event_date)` with `ORDER BY (tenant_id, campaign_id, event_date)` keeps the sparse 8,192-row primary index under 200MB in RAM. Queries touching 4 columns scan 96% less data than PostgreSQL and complete in 65ms p95 with 14:1 ZSTD compression.
